unit.title: Strategies
unit.description: From buy and hold to day trading: what the evidence says about each strategy

steps.title: The boring strategy that works
steps.body:
Buy a broad, cheap index and **hold it for decades**, adding money regularly.

According to SPIVA (end of 2025), **97 %** of European equity funds lagged their index over 10 years. If hardly anyone beats the index, buying the index already puts you ahead of almost everyone.

steps.title: Time is on your side
steps.body:
S&P 500, approximate history. Share of periods with a gain:

• 1 day: just over 50 %
• 1 year: around 73 %
• 10 years: around 90 %
• 20 years: almost 100 % since 1926

Careful: that's US history. Japan took 34 years to get back to its 1989 high.

steps.title: Let time do the work
steps.body: Put in €100 a month at 7 % (an example, not a promise) and compare 10 years with 30.
steps.tip: Most of the result comes in the last few years.

steps.title: Missing the best days
steps.body: J.P. Morgan: $10,000 in the S&P 500 from 2005 to 2024 turned into about **$71,750**. Anyone who missed just the 10 best days ended up with about **$32,871**. And 7 of those 10 days came very close to the worst ones.
steps.key: In the stock market, time in the market beats timing the market.
steps.tip: A boring portfolio is a portfolio that works.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body:
Investing **the same amount every month**, whatever happens (*dollar-cost averaging*).

Example: €100 a month for 5 months with the price at 10 → 8 → 5 → 8 → €10. You buy 10 + 12.5 + 20 + 12.5 + 10 = **65 units** for €500. Average price: **€7.69**, even though it started and finished at €10.

steps.title: What about a lump sum?
steps.body:
Vanguard: over 10-year periods, investing **everything at once** beat spreading it out **about two times out of three**. With the MSCI World (1976–2022), after one year, **68 %** of the time.

The reason: the market goes up more often than it goes down. But spreading it out reduces regret if it falls right afterwards.

steps.title: Invest every month
steps.body: Try €150 a month for 20 years at an example 6 % a year. Compare what you put in with the result.
steps.tip: What moves the result most is starting early and not stopping.

steps.title: Key takeaway
steps.body: With a lump sum, a reasonable middle ground is to spread it over **6–12 months** with automatic contributions. What doesn't work is waiting «for it to drop»: nobody knows where the bottom is.
steps.key: All at once usually wins more often; bit by bit reduces regret. What matters is starting and not stopping.
steps.tip: Investing every month is like climbing stairs: what matters is not stopping.

steps.title: Price and value
steps.body:
«Price is what you pay; value is what you get» (Warren Buffett).

A value investor estimates what a business is **worth** (profits, cash, debt, competitive advantages) and only buys if the **price** is clearly below it.

Graham, his mentor, talked about **Mr Market**: a moody business partner who some days asks an absurd price and other days practically gives you his share.

steps.title: Margin of safety
steps.body:
Value is always an **estimate**. That's why you buy with a cushion: the **margin of safety**.

If you estimate a share is worth €19.60 and it trades at €15, the price is 23 % below your estimate. If you're a little wrong, you still have room.

steps.title: What it isn't
steps.body: Value isn't buying whatever has fallen a lot or has the lowest P/E. A low P/E can be a business in decline: a **value trap**. And the style can spend years lagging the market.
steps.key: Buying businesses for less than they're worth, with a margin in case you're wrong.
steps.tip: An excellent company bought too expensively can be a bad investment.

steps.title: How a dividend works
steps.body:
When a company pays a €1 dividend, the share price drops by roughly €1 that day (the **ex-dividend date**). You're no richer: you have €1 in cash and €1 less in shares.

And in Spain that euro is taxed under IRPF (Spanish income tax) at 19 % to 30 %; the payer usually withholds 19 % up front.

steps.title: Two ratios
steps.body:
• **Dividend yield** = dividend per share ÷ price. It pays €0.50 and trades at €15: **3.3 %**.
• ***Payout ratio*** = dividend ÷ earnings per share. Consistently above 80–90 %, the dividend may be at risk.

steps.title: The high-yield trap
steps.body:
A 12 % dividend isn't usually a bargain: often the price has fallen because the market expects a **cut**. Check that it's covered by earnings and cash flow.

To build wealth, **accumulating** funds reinvest without paying tax until you sell.
steps.key: A dividend isn't free money: it comes out of the company's value. What matters is total return.
steps.tip: A sky-high dividend is sometimes a warning, not a gift.

steps.title: The idea
steps.body:
Buy what has been rising for a while and get out when the trend breaks.

It has backing: **3–12 month** trends have tended to persist in shares, indices, bonds, currencies and commodities (Jegadeesh and Titman; Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen; Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen, with data going back to 1880).

steps.title: The price of following trends
steps.body:
• It's right **less than half** the time: lots of small losses and a few big gains.
• In **sideways** markets it gives false signals again and again.
• Sharp reversals catch it in the trade.

Its edge depends on cutting losses quickly and letting gains run.

steps.title: Key takeaway
steps.body: A typical rule: buy when the price rises above its long-term moving average, with a stop below the latest higher low, and raise the stop as it moves up.
steps.key: Momentum is one of the most studied anomalies, but it only works with discipline and risk management.
steps.tip: The trend is your friend… until it turns. That's why you always use a stop.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body:
Trades lasting **days to weeks**, usually on the daily chart. You aim to catch one leg of the move: buy on a pullback or at a support within a trend and get out near resistance.

It doesn't require watching the screen all day, but it does mean checking the market daily.

steps.title: Its risks
steps.body:
• **Gaps:** you hold positions overnight and over the weekend; an earnings report or a piece of news can open the price far from your stop.
• **Costs:** commission and *spread* on every trade.
• **Noise:** the shorter the timeframe, the more false signals.

steps.title: Key takeaway
steps.body: Every trade needs its stop, its target and its size at 1 % risk before you enter. Better not to hold big positions going into earnings.
steps.key: Swing: legs lasting days or weeks, with a structural stop and a reward/risk ratio of 2:1 or more.
steps.tip: In swing trading the weekend counts too: size your positions with gaps in mind.

u25l7.title: Day trading: what the data says

steps.title: The studies
steps.body:
• **Brazil** (Chague, De-Losso and Giovannetti, 2020): of those who *day traded* index futures for more than 300 days, **97 % lost money**. Only 1.1 % earned more than the minimum wage.
• **Taiwan** (Barber, Lee, Liu and Odean): fewer than **1 %** of *day traders* manage to make money predictably and persistently after fees.

steps.title: Why it happens
steps.body:
• **Costs:** every trade pays commission and *spread*. With lots of trades a day, they eat up any small edge.
• **Competition:** on the other side there are professionals and algorithms with better data and near-zero costs.
• **Noise:** on minute charts, most moves mean nothing.

steps.title: Key takeaway
steps.body: On social media you only see screenshots of wins, never the full track record. And people selling courses make money from the courses, not necessarily from trading.
steps.key: The vast majority of people who day trade consistently lose money.
steps.tip: If someone makes a living teaching you to make a living from trading, ask yourself what they really live on.

steps.title: What leverage is
steps.body:
Trading with more money than you have. With **1:10**, €1,000 controls €10,000:

• The asset rises 5 %: you make €500, **+50 %**.
• It falls 5 %: you lose €500, **−50 %**.
• It falls 10 %: you lose **everything**.

On top of that, holding it overnight costs daily **financing**.

steps.title: CFDs: the official warning
steps.body:
A **CFD** tracks the price changes of an asset with leverage, without you owning it. The CNMV requires brokers to show this warning:

«CFDs are complex instruments and come with a high risk of losing money rapidly due to leverage. Between 74 and 89 % of retail investor accounts lose money when trading CFDs.»

steps.title: EU limits and shorts
steps.body:
Since 2018 (ESMA): maximum leverage of **1:30** on major currency pairs, 1:20 on major indices, 1:5 on shares and **1:2 on crypto**; positions are closed if margin drops below 50 %; you can't lose more than you deposited.

**Going short** means selling something you don't own to buy it back cheaper. The loss is **unlimited**: the price can rise with no ceiling (GameStop, 2021).

steps.title: The course's recommendation
steps.body: While you're learning: **no leverage and no shorting**. If you ever use them, do it with a small part of your capital, always with a stop, and with size calculated on the total exposure, not on the margin.
steps.key: Leverage multiplies gains and losses equally, but big losses take you out of the game.
steps.tip: Leverage doesn't make you a better trader: it just makes your mistakes arrive sooner.

steps.title: There's no single best one for everyone
steps.body:
The strategy has to fit:

• **Your time:** minutes a month or hours a day?
• **Your horizon:** when will you need the money?
• **Your temperament:** what fall could you take without selling?
• **Your knowledge:** can you read a set of accounts or a chart?

The best strategy is the one **you'll be able to stick to** when things go badly.

steps.title: Core and satellite
steps.body: Lots of people separate a long-term **core portfolio** (diversified, cheap, automatic) from a **small part** for speculating or learning, with a written limit they could lose entirely.
steps.key: The boring core first; the excitement, if any, with a small, capped part.
steps.tip: Choose the strategy you'd still follow during a 30 % fall.

u25l1-1.prompt: This is how the S&P 500 was doing up to March 2009. What trend do you see? (S&P 500 · weekly closes · up to 02/03/2009)
u25l1-1.explanation: A fall of more than 50 % from 2007: the moment when the most people gave up on «buy and hold».

u25l1-2.prompt: March 2009: after the worst crisis in decades, lots of people sell «so as not to lose any more». What did the S&P 500 do next?
u25l1-2.explanation: Those who held on (or kept investing) recovered. Those who sold in the panic turned a temporary fall into a permanent loss.
u25l1-2.horizon: the next year and a half

u25l1-3.prompt: According to J.P. Morgan, $10,000 invested in the S&P 500 from 2005 to 2024 ended up as $71,750; missing the 10 best days, as $32,871. What's the difference?
u25l1-3.explanation: 71,750 − 32,871 = $38,879: more than half the result came down to 10 days.

u25l1-4.prompt: Match each time frame with the historical share of periods with a gain in the S&P 500.
u25l1-4.explanation: The longer the time frame, the lower the chance of losing in US history. It's not a law of physics.

u25l1-5.prompt: Buy and hold guarantees a gain over 20 years in any country.
u25l1-5.explanation: Japan took 34 years to get back to its 1989 high. That's why you diversify across countries.

u25l1-6.prompt: December 1989: the Japanese stock market is the biggest in the world and has been rising for years. What did the Nikkei 225 do next?
u25l1-6.explanation: The Nikkei took 34 years to get back to that high. Buy and hold works better with a global index than with a single country.

u25l1-7.prompt: March 2020: the S&P 500 falls 34 % in a month because of covid. Pablo has an index fund for his retirement, 35 years away. What does he do?
options: Takes out a loan to buy more
Sells everything and waits for it to pass
Sticks to his plan and his contributions
u25l1-7.explanation: Buy and hold means sitting through the falls: that's where the strategy is won or lost.
feedback: Investing with debt in the middle of a crisis can force you to sell at the worst moment.
The index got back to its high in about 5 months. Pablo would have missed the strongest rebounds.
Good: his contributions bought cheap and within a few months the index was back at its highs.

u25l1-8.prompt: Quick one: according to SPIVA, what share of European equity funds lagged their index over 10 years?
u25l1-8.explanation: End of 2025. And almost none of those that beat it do it again.

u25l1-9.prompt: What does buy and hold need to work? Select all that apply.
u25l1-9.explanation: Selling at every fall is exactly the opposite: it makes you miss the rebounds.

u25l1-10.prompt: What do you reply to Lumi?
options: Better look for the share that rises most this year
Boring isn't bad: it's the strategy with the most long-term evidence
u25l1-10.explanation: Excitement doesn't pay: what pays is staying invested, diversified and with low costs for years.
feedback: That's gambling: most individual shares do worse than the index.
OK, OK. Boring for long-term money, and the excitement with a small part.
Well, according to SPIVA, 97 % of European active funds do worse than the index over 10 years…
lines: Buy and hold is for grandparents 👴

u25l2-1.prompt: You invest €100 a month and the price goes through 10, 8, 5, 8 and €10. How many units do you have in total?

u25l2-2.prompt: With those 65 units for €500, what's your average purchase price? (round to two decimal places)
u25l2-2.explanation: 500 ÷ 65 ≈ €7.69. Since it ends at €10, you make 30 % without the price having risen.

u25l2-3.prompt: September 2008. You start putting €200 a month into an S&P 500 fund. What did the index do over the following months?
u25l2-3.explanation: With regular contributions, when the price falls you buy more units with the same money: falls work in your favour if you don't stop.

u25l2-4.prompt: July 2012: the IBEX 35 has had years of crisis and hardly anyone wants to invest in Spain. If you were investing every month, what happened next?
u25l2-4.explanation: Anyone investing every month bought lots of cheap units at the worst of the crisis. DCA doesn't require guessing the bottom.
u25l2-4.horizon: the next year and a half

u25l2-5.prompt: Ana inherits €30,000 to invest for the long term. She knows from experience that if she invests it all and it falls 20 % the next month, she'd sell everything out of nerves. Which option fits best with what she knows about herself?
options: Spread it over 6–12 months with automatic contributions
Wait for the market to drop
u25l2-5.explanation: The best strategy is the one you'll be able to stick to. Waiting for «the right moment» is usually the worst.
feedback: A good middle ground: she gets into the market without the fear of doing it all on the worst day.
Nobody knows when it'll drop: while she waits, the market could rise 30 %.
Statistically it wins about 2 times out of 3, but Ana already knows she'd bail out in a fall, and that would be the worst outcome.

u25l2-6.prompt: According to Vanguard, investing a lump sum all at once beat spreading it out about two times out of three.
u25l2-6.explanation: Because the market goes up more often than it goes down: waiting usually costs you.

u25l2-7.prompt: Why does investing all at once win more often than spreading it out?
options: Because the market goes up more often than it goes down
u25l2-7.explanation: Every month you wait, the money still to be invested isn't in the market.

u25l2-8.prompt: Is it an advantage of regular contributions or of investing all at once?
options: All the money works from day one
It fits with getting paid a salary every month
It reduces regret if it falls right afterwards
u25l2-8.explanation: Both are valid: what doesn't work is trying to guess the timing.

u25l2-9.prompt: Regular contributions guarantee buying at the lowest price.
u25l2-9.explanation: You buy at a range of prices: your average price is reasonable, but not the lowest.

u25l2-10.prompt: Investing the same amount every month, whatever happens, is called ____.

u25l3-1.prompt: You estimate a share is worth €20 and it trades at €15. What margin of safety do you have relative to your estimated value?

u25l3-2.prompt: You estimate a company is worth €40 per share and you demand a 30 % margin of safety. What's the most you'd pay?

options: The head of the stock exchange
A moody business partner who offers you a different price every day
u25l3-3.explanation: You don't have to listen to him: you can take advantage of his panic days and not buy from him on his euphoric days.

u25l3-4.prompt: Because of a general panic, a company with stable profits, little debt and loyal customers falls 30 % in a month without its business having changed. How does a value investor see it?
options: Sells: if it's falling, something bad is going on
Checks whether the business is still the same and whether there's now a margin of safety
Buys with all their money without looking at anything
u25l3-4.explanation: A value investor separates the price (which changes every day) from the value of the business (which changes slowly).
feedback: That's letting Mr Market decide for you, right on his panic day.
Good: if the value hasn't changed but the price has, there may be an opportunity. You check first.
Without analysis or diversification it isn't value investing: it's gambling.

u25l3-5.prompt: Bruno finds a share with a P/E of 4. Sales have been falling for 5 years, debt keeps rising and the sector is disappearing. What is it?
options: A sure bargain because of its low P/E
u25l3-5.explanation: A low ratio isn't enough: you have to check whether the business is holding up.
feedback: Its sales are falling: that's the opposite.
The low P/E reflects that the market expects profits to keep falling.
Exactly: cheap isn't the same as undervalued. The business is shrinking.

u25l3-6.prompt: Match each concept with its meaning.
u25l3-6.explanation: These are the basic building blocks of Graham and Buffett's value investing.
right: An advantage that protects the business from competitors
The cushion between that value and the price
What you estimate the business is worth

u25l3-7.prompt: A low P/E always means the share is cheap.
u25l3-7.explanation: It could be a company in decline or one with a one-off inflated profit. Compare it with the sector and with its growth.

u25l3-8.prompt: The value style beats the market every year.
u25l3-8.explanation: It has had long periods, of more than a decade, lagging the market. It takes a lot of patience.

u25l3-9.prompt: Buffett: «Price is what you pay; ____ is what you get».
u25l3-9.explanation: Price and value aren't the same thing: value investing lives off that difference.

u25l3-10.prompt: Which signs point to a possible value trap? Select all that apply.
options: Stable profits and a high ROIC
u25l3-10.explanation: Stable profits and a high return on capital are signs of quality, not of a trap.

u25l3-11.prompt: What do you say to Lumi?
options: Yes, the more it falls, the better
Value is buying whatever is rising most
What matters is what the business is worth, not what it used to trade at
u25l3-11.explanation: Value compares price with value, not today's price with yesterday's.
feedback: That's anchoring: the fact that it used to be €100 says nothing about what it's worth today.
That sounds more like momentum, which is a different strategy.
Ah, OK: first I estimate the value, and only if the price is well below it is there a margin.
lines: Value investing means buying whatever has fallen the most, right? 📉
This share was at €100 and now it's at €40: bargain!

u25l4-1.prompt: A share trades at €15 and pays a €0.50 dividend a year. What's its dividend yield? (round to one decimal place)

u25l4-2.prompt: A company earns €2 per share and pays a €1.80 dividend. What's its payout ratio?
u25l4-2.explanation: 1.80 ÷ 2 = 0.9 → 90 %: it pays out almost everything it earns. If profits fall, the dividend is at risk.

u25l4-3.prompt: You receive €1,000 gross in dividends from Spanish companies and 19 % is withheld. How much reaches your account?
u25l4-3.explanation: 1,000 × (1 − 0.19) = €810. Then, in your tax return, it's adjusted to your bracket.

u25l4-4.prompt: Select the messages that are a scam or an obvious trap.
options: Exclusive fund: 1 % dividend every month guaranteed, no risk. Transfer to this account today.
Live off dividends with just €1,000 💸 Join my paid group and I'll tell you which ones.
The company you hold shares in will pay a dividend of €0.40 per share. Ex-dividend date: the 12th.
Reminder: dividends are declared as investment income in your IRPF (Spanish income tax) return.
🔥 Share paying a GUARANTEED 15 % dividend. Today only, limited places.
u25l4-4.explanation: Promises of guaranteed dividends, urgency and «living off your investments with €1,000» are signs of fraud. No share guarantees its dividend.

u25l4-5.prompt: When a company pays a dividend, its share price usually drops by roughly that amount.
u25l4-5.explanation: The money leaves the company: your total wealth doesn't change by receiving it.

u25l4-6.prompt: A share offers a 13 % dividend. What should you check first?
options: How many followers it has on social media
Whether earnings and cash cover the dividend, and why the price has fallen so much
u25l4-6.explanation: A yield like that usually means the market expects a cut.

u25l4-7.prompt: Is it a feature of an accumulating fund or a distributing fund?
options: It pays the dividends into your account
You don't pay tax until you sell
Useful if you need a regular income
u25l4-7.explanation: While you're building wealth, accumulating funds are usually more tax-efficient.

u25l4-8.prompt: Quick one: what can a 95 % payout ratio over several years indicate?
options: That the company is growing very fast
That the dividend may be at risk
u25l4-8.explanation: It pays out almost everything it earns: little room if profits fall.

u25l4-9.prompt: Bruno is looking for income. He's torn between a company with a 12 % dividend, falling profits and rising debt, and another with a 3 % dividend comfortably covered by earnings. What's the more prudent criterion?
options: Pick whichever has risen most this month
Look at how sustainable the dividend is, not just its size
The 12 % one: it pays four times as much
u25l4-9.explanation: What matters is total return and that the dividend is sustainable.
feedback: That says nothing about whether the dividend is sustainable.
Good: a covered, stable dividend is worth more than a high one at risk.
If it cuts the dividend and the share falls, Bruno loses income and capital at the same time.

u25l4-10.prompt: The day a share starts trading without the right to the dividend is called the ____ date.
u25l4-10.explanation: On that day the price drops by roughly the amount paid out as a dividend.

u25l5-1.prompt: What trend do you see in this real chart? (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · March–May 2026)
u25l5-1.explanation: Higher and higher highs and lows: this is trend-follower territory.

u25l5-2.prompt: And in this one? (NVIDIA · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2025)
u25l5-2.explanation: Lower and lower highs and lows: a long-only trend follower would stay out.

u25l5-3.prompt: Last chart. What trend is there? (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · July–September 2025)
u25l5-3.explanation: No clear direction: this is where trend strategies suffer false signals.

u25l5-4.prompt: This asset had been rising. As a trend follower, what do you think it did over the following sessions?
u25l5-4.explanation: A trend persisting more often than it reverses doesn't mean it always does: that's why you use a stop.

u25l5-5.prompt: Another real chart of an index. Does it go up or down afterwards?
u25l5-5.explanation: The momentum edge is statistical, across many trades. In a single case, anything can happen.

u25l5-6.prompt: Over what time frame have trends tended to persist according to momentum studies?
u25l5-6.explanation: That's the horizon of most studies, across many markets and going back more than a century.

u25l5-7.prompt: Trend strategies usually win most of their trades.
u25l5-7.explanation: They're usually right less than half the time: they make money because their wins are much bigger than their losses.

u25l5-8.prompt: A trend system is right 35 % of the time, wins 3R on average and loses 1R. What's its expectancy?

u25l5-9.prompt: Quick one: where does a trend follower suffer most?
u25l5-9.explanation: With no clear direction, it gets in and out again and again with small losses.

u25l5-10.prompt: Put the steps of a simple trend-following rule in order.
options: Enter when your rule's signal is triggered
Work out the size with 1 % risk
Put the stop below the latest higher low
Raise the stop as the trend moves on
Check there's an uptrend (higher highs and higher lows)
u25l5-10.explanation: Without the stop and the size, no trend rule survives its reversals.

u25l6-1.prompt: Swing trade: you have €10,000 and risk 1 % at most. Choose the stop and amount.
u25l6-1.explanation: Stop below the recent low and size calculated with that stop. The rest is up to the market.

u25l6-2.prompt: Another trade, now with a €5,000 account. Same limit: 1 % at most.
u25l6-2.explanation: If the price goes against you, the stop limits the loss to what you planned. That's why you decide it before entering.

u25l6-3.prompt: Swing trade on an index. Place the stop for this buy.
u25l6-3.explanation: Below the recent low: if it breaks, the pullback has turned into something else.

u25l6-4.prompt: Now place the target for this buy.
u25l6-4.explanation: Near the previous high, where selling tends to show up. Compare it with the distance to the stop.

u25l6-5.prompt: A swing trader looks for ranges and trends. What do you see here? (NVIDIA · closes every 3 sessions · December 2025 – February 2026)
u25l6-5.explanation: In a sideways market, the swing trader buys near the floor of the range and sells near the ceiling, with a stop below the floor.

u25l6-6.prompt: In a range, the target for a buy usually goes near the ceiling. Tap the highest point. (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · September–November 2024)
u25l6-6.explanation: The ceiling of the range is where selling showed up before.

u25l6-7.prompt: Match each style with its typical time frame.
u25l6-7.explanation: The shorter the time frame, the more noise and the more costs for every euro earned.
right: Minutes or hours; closes the same day

u25l6-8.prompt: What risk does swing trading have that day trading doesn't?
options: Price gaps between one session and the next
u25l6-8.explanation: Because you hold positions overnight, the price can open far from your stop.

u25l6-9.prompt: Swing trading is usually done on 1-minute charts.
u25l6-9.explanation: It usually uses the daily chart: trades lasting days to weeks.

u25l6-10.prompt: Swing: you enter at €30, stop at €28.50 and target at €34.50. If it reaches the target, how many R do you make?

u25l7-1.prompt: According to the Brazil study, most people who day traded for more than 300 days made money.

u25l7-2.prompt: In that Brazil study, what percentage earned more than the minimum wage?
u25l7-2.explanation: 1.1 %: even among the few who made money, almost none made enough to live on.

u25l7-3.prompt: In Taiwan, fewer than 1 % of day traders manage to make money predictably after fees.
u25l7-3.explanation: Barber, Lee, Liu and Odean, with data from the Taiwan stock exchange from 1992 to 2006.

u25l7-4.prompt: Of those who day traded for more than 300 days in Brazil, ____ lost money.

u25l7-5.prompt: You make 4 trades a day and each one costs you €5 in commission and spread. Over 250 market days, how much do you pay in costs?
u25l7-5.explanation: 4 × 5 × 250 = €5,000: before you've made anything, you already have to win that back.

u25l7-6.prompt: Why do most day traders lose? Select all that apply.
options: The costs of trading so much
u25l7-6.explanation: It isn't banned: the maths simply works against you.

u25l7-7.prompt: An influencer shows screenshots of €3,000 made in one day and sells a €500 course to «make a living from trading». What do you do?
options: Ask for their full, verified track record, and remember the studies
Copy their trades with borrowed money
Buy the course, the screenshots prove it
u25l7-7.explanation: Screenshots of wins prove nothing: what counts is the full track record, including costs.
feedback: Good: chances are they don't have one. And the data says 97 % of persistent traders lose.
